title: Anthropic IPO Is Chance to End Deferred Stock Pay, FT Argues
excerpt: The Financial Times used Anthropic's listing to argue, as opinion, that regulators should stop letting companies defer stock-based compensation costs, a practice that leaves $23.7 billion of Anthropic employee pay to be recognized only after its IPO.
body:
• In an opinion piece published on November 4, the Financial Times argued that, to protect retail investors, regulators should stop permitting the deferral of stock-based employee compensation costs, using Anthropic's listing as the occasion to make the case.
  • Anthropic's S-1 shows why the issue is large: it recorded $2.2 billion of stock-based compensation in the first half of 2026, would book a further $2.9 billion charge at the IPO, and has $23.7 billion more to recognize over about 2.1 years.
  • The deferral exists because many Anthropic restricted stock units vest only on a liquidity event, so the expense was not booked while an IPO was not considered probable.
  • For readers considering the shares: Anthropic's adjusted operating income adds stock compensation back, so adjusted and GAAP results tell different stories, and the offering's price range is still blank.

Anthropic's path to the public markets should prompt a change in how employee stock pay is accounted for before a listing, the Financial Times argued in an opinion piece published on November 4. Its stated argument is narrow and specific: "To protect retail investors, we should stop permitting the deferral of stock-based employee compensation costs." That is the newspaper's opinion; no rule change has been announced.

The piece arrives after Anthropic, the maker of the Claude models, made its registration statement public on October 26, 2026. The filing lists the shares on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker ANT, with Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley leading the offering, and leaves the price range and share count blank. Market expectations cited in coverage put the valuation between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion; those are others' expectations, not a price set by the company.

What the filing actually reports

Anthropic recorded revenue of $16.3 billion in the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion a year earlier, according to breakdowns of the S-1 by Mostly Metrics and CEOWORLD Magazine. On a GAAP basis, the first half was still an operating loss of $693 million. The headline net loss of $80.7 billion is mostly a non-cash charge from marking convertible notes to a higher valuation, not cash spent.

Adjusted figures look different, and the difference is the FT's subject. Adjusted operating income for the first half was $1.6 billion, a 10 percent margin, according to the S-1 breakdown, because the adjustments add back stock compensation and non-cash charitable donations. The adjusted number shows a profit; GAAP shows a loss. Both come from the same filing.

How the deferral works

Many of Anthropic's restricted stock units require two conditions to vest: time served and a liquidity event. Until an IPO is considered probable, the related expense cannot be booked. The cost of work already done therefore sits off the income statement during the private years and arrives in a concentrated block once the company lists.

The scale makes Anthropic a test case. It recorded $1.2 billion of stock-based compensation in 2025 and $2.2 billion in the first six months of 2026. Had the IPO closed on June 30, it would have booked a one-time charge of $2.9 billion, with a further $23.7 billion to be recognized over about 2.1 years, plus another $3.1 billion on other awards. Those are accounting charges, not cash payouts, but they are real costs of compensating about 5,300 people, and they will shape the earnings new shareholders see after the listing.

What the argument would change

On the FT's argument as stated, ending the deferral would mean the cost is recognized closer to when the work is done, so post-IPO accounts would not absorb years of it at once. The piece, on the evidence available outside the FT paywall, does not set out a detailed replacement rule, and this report does not attribute one to it. A separate point in the same filing adds to what new investors must price: some non-founder directors, officers and employees may sell up to 10 percent of their holdings from the first trading day, 35 percent more after 2026 results, and the rest at the earlier of first-quarter 2027 results or day 180, according to CEOWORLD's reading of the prospectus, rather than the full 180-day hold large listings usually impose.

What to watch next

The next document that matters is an amended filing with a price range and share count. Until it appears, valuation figures in circulation remain other people's estimates. For a reader weighing exposure to a large AI listing, the practical lesson is a reading habit, not a buy or sell call: compare the adjusted profit with the GAAP result, and check how much stock compensation has yet to be recognized. In Anthropic's case, that amount is $23.7 billion over about 2.1 years, plus $3.1 billion on other awards.
